newsitem.title: UK: High-flying Russian debt prices still safe - analysts.
newsitem.headline: High-flying Russian debt prices still safe - analysts.

text.p: Jonathan Thatcher

Turbulent politics and slow economic growth have not stopped Russian debt prices outperforming almost every other market this year and analysts said it is not over yet despite the latest Kremlin squabble.

If anything, Thursday's dismissal of security chief Alexander Lebed, accused of organising a "creeping coup", has ended political uncertainty and given investors more confidence in President Boris Yeltsin, the analysts said on Friday.
"We don't think this changes Russia as a credit in the medium or long term. We think it's a buy," Paribas Capital Markets analyst Stuart Brown said.

The price of the $32 billion worth of old Soviet debt -- in the name of Vneshekonombank and close to being restructured -- has surged 150 percent this year, outstripping virtually anything else in its class.

But the latest doubts do mean that prices may not be heading up quite as fast to the highs many banks were predicting only two weeks ago when the Vneshekonombank dollar debt hit a record high of 80 percent of face value.
It is now hovering just under 77 cents, after slumping to 74 on Thursday morning.
"The immediate sell-off reflects mild alarm, but equally some profit-taking after the exceptional run-up in prices since Augus," Merrill Lynch analyst Dan McGovern said.
A price recovery may be slow but there is still room for it to move higher, he added.

He noted that over $2 billion in cash is due to be paid out once the commercial debt restructuring deal with bank creditors is completed. That is expected within a matter of months once auditors sort out exactly who owes what.
"Vnesh is probably the safest thing to be in," West Merchant Bank economist Lina Takla.
But the outlook is far from settled and the high credit ratings awarded to Russia earlier this month are beginning to look overdone, she said.

However, most analysts believe the Lebed issue should not get in the way of either the debt restructuring or Russia's planned Eurobond issue, which many have speculated would be priced relatively cheaply for Russia at a spread of 350 points.
"The inaugural Eurobond appears on schedule for November...Lebed's ouster should not affect the bond," said McGovern.

"If you think, which I do, that this is just a squabble among politicians jockeying ahead of the next presidential election then this is no big deal. If you think there is going to be a coup, then sure, get out," a senior European bank trader said.
"Even if the Vnesh deal is delayed for a few months, I wouldn't be upset," he added.
Some traders remain worried that a Lebed completely outside the restraints of office could prove an even greater nuisance to the government.
"People are nervous. It is going to stay volatile until Yelstin's operation and he is seen to be recovering," one said.
Brown of Paribas said that in the short-term and after such a heady rise in prices, it was inevitable that investors would want to put some of their profits in the bank.
"There is a temptation for many houses to sell," he said.
